newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iran to invite Saudi King Fahd to Tehran.
newsitem.headline: Iran to invite Saudi King Fahd to Tehran.

text.p: Iran's Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati on Sunday began a tour of 10 countries including Saudi Arabia where he plans to invite King Fahd to visit Tehran.
The Islamic republic's media reported his trip to Damascus and said he would also go to Turkey, Sudan, Uganda, the Czech republic and Gulf Arab states including Saudi Arabia.

President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani is inviting heads of Moslem states and governments to visit the Iranian capital in December for a summit of the Organisation of Islamic Conference (OIC), the world's largest Moslem body.
Velayati's visit to Riyadh, his first since 1993, poses a diplomatic dilemma for Saudi Arabia's royal family, Gulf-based diplomatic sources said.
The kingdom is home to two of Islam's most sacred shrines in the closed cities of Mecca and Medina and its commercial capital Jeddah is the headquarters of the 51-nation OIC.

A Western diplomat in Tehran said Iranian leaders were worried about possible lack of support for the December summit because of an out-of-session summit timed to coincide with the golden jubilee of Pakistan's independence on March 23.

"They're now getting very worried that people aren't going to bother to come in December. Velayati has just come back from a tour of Southeast Asia getting people to sign up for it and to say how important it is and we're going to come," he said.

"The thought of King Fahd turning up in Iran...that would really be something if they reckoned they could pull that one off," he told Reuters by telephone. "Knowing the Iranians I wouldn't be at all surprised if they're trying very hard.
"It may well be that even if King Fahd isn't coming Velayati has gone to lobby for high-level attendance," the diplomat said.
Another diplomatic source in Tehran said Iran wanted to have a good gathering at the summit, which takes place every four years.

"According to reports the Saudis were not very enamoured about it and they would like to find some excuse to put it off. Even if they attended at a lower level the problem for the Saudis would be that Iran would assume the chairmanship of the OIC for four years."

"Even if there are not many heads of state in Tehran it would still be called a summit and the Iranians would still become chairman. This prospect is dreaded by the Saudis and their friends in the Gulf. There are lots of things happening to find some solution," the source added.
"Saudi Arabia's presence would be crucial because the Saudis have the capacity to make or break the conference."

Relations between radical Shi'ite Iran and the Sunni-ruled kingdom are already uneasy and they are bracing for a period of heightened tension over the annual haj pilgrimage to the holy cities of Meca and Medina.
Iran insists that its pilgrims hold political rallies to denounce Israel and the United States during haj, which all Moslems are expected to perform once.
This year's pilgrimage falls in mid-April.
Saudi Arabia's conservative royal family insists that haj, one of the pillars of Islam and the world's largest religious gathering, is a sacred affair and should not be politicised.
Saudi security forces clashed in 1987 with demonstrators in an Iranian-led rally in the streets of Mecca, killing about 400 people, mainly Iranians. Iran boycotted haj for three years.
Saudi authorities have repeatedly warned pilgrims they would face tough punishment if they carried political material to haj.

Riyadh and Tehran, two of the world's biggest oil exporters, are also at odds over the presence of U.S. and other Western forces in the Gulf. Iran is critical of the Western presence, including about 5,000 U.S. forces in Saudi Arabia, which it says contributes to regional tension.
Saudi Arabia and its Gulf Arab allies have accused Iran of interfering in their internal affairs, which Iran denies, and voiced concern over its arms build-up.
